book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

chapters.file: ch80 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Closing track-list of Chapter 9, pairing songs from Exile on Main St. with Liz Phair's song-for-song answer Exile in Guyville under the heading of romantic and sexual exile. 'Loving Cup' meets 'Mesmerizing' as unrequited lust from male and female sides, 'Happy' meets 'Fuck and Run' on whether lasting attachments are possible, and 'Ventilator Blues' meets 'Divorce Song' on the loaded-gun violence of failing relationships. The pairing argues Phair and Jagger/Richards map the same territory of oversexed dissatisfaction from opposite perspectives.

chapters.file: ch81 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy.md
ch82 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy.md
ch83 - Chapter 10 - When the Whip Comes Down.md
chapters.relation: Randall Auxier opens Chapter 10 by defining rock'n'roll as pent-up energy stored against its tendency to diffuse, then released in little bursts between sixty and 160 times per minute in groups of four. Borrowing Keith Richards's word 'discipline,' he argues rock requires chaining the moment and whipping it 'until it feels bad enough to be good,' so that every explosion destroys as much as it creates. Even the gods, he concludes, must die a little death at the end of every bar.

chapters.file: ch84 - Mad Men.md
chapters.relation: Auxier argues rock periodically cleanses itself of commercial packaging, citing Hall and Oates versus Johnny Rotten and Culture Club versus Kurt Cobain as each era's corrective upheaval. The Madison Avenue 'Mad Men' sell kids sanitized three-minute morsels like Herman's Hermits, but the kids' own bottled energy finds ground anyway, and once they 'get their ya-yas out' the packaged pop stops working. The Stones enter as the real rhythm that arrives when something has to be put 'under the whip.'

chapters.file: ch85 - “It”.md
chapters.relation: Auxier distinguishes celebrity from 'It,' the untheorizable path to ground that lets a performer channel atmospheric energy, noting it lives just as well in obscure bar bands as in stars. He defines 'It' as the what-ness and that-ness of 'he has It,' a circuit completed when the right components are hooked up and tied down in the right order, and names this inquiry musical metaphysics. The chapter ends by recruiting Alfred North Whitehead, whose process philosophy of time and energy will supply the theory.

chapters.file: ch86 - Musical Metaphysics.md
chapters.relation: Auxier presents Whitehead's claim that there are no things, only rhythmic patterns of vibration: molecules are 'performances,' and quoted passages from Process and Reality on the rolling stone dismantle materialist atomism. He maps the rhythm section onto Whitehead's phases of concrescence — Keith the datum, Charlie the synthesis, Bill the 'satisfaction' — with grooves and riffs as the protonic and electronic rhythms of intensity. The upshot, that what we do makes us what we are, explains why the Stones' rhythm section is the best ever.

chapters.file: ch87 - The Sum of the Parts.md
chapters.relation: Auxier asks why 'It' works only when the Stones are together, testing the band's fifty-year experiment against lineup changes: Brian Jones proved dispensable, the second guitar modular, yet Bill Wyman's 1992 departure genuinely weakened the circuit. He claims Keith-Charlie-Bill in series (data-synthesis-satisfaction) are the real power source, with Jagger merely the light bulb that draws the current — the Keith-Charlie-Bill band would have been famous without Mick, but Mick is nothing without the circuit. A lithium analogy renders the band loosely bound, unstable and flammable, and the chapter closes by insisting Charlie interprets Keith and Bill interprets Charlie, in that order.

chapters.file: ch88 - A Date with Keith.md
chapters.relation: Auxier casts Keith Richards as Prometheus with a five-stringed lightning rod who pulls grooves and riffs down from the atmosphere, sloppily out of tune yet almost never off. Against critics who rank him below Clapton, Hendrix, Page and Beck, he argues that originating body-moving grooves and unforgettable riffs is harder than flashy lead work — the riff and groove are the batter and bake of the rock'n'roll cake. Keith's greatness lies in being the promethean point of origin every band needs.

chapters.file: ch89 - Maestro Tempo and Mr. Groove.md
chapters.relation: Auxier distinguishes finding a groove again — pulling it up from the body's stored repetition, as the bar-band 'grooves guy' does before a song — from the conductor's interpretive choice of tempo. He personifies Maestro Tempo as a proper suitor of Miss Sound (Herman's Hermits territory) against Mr. Groove, who operates independently of how things sound so long as the feel dominates. In rock, he concludes, Sound must conform to Groove rather than the reverse.

chapters.file: ch90 - Who Could Hang a Name on You.md
chapters.relation: Auxier separates discovering a groove — Whitehead's 'self-creative act,' explicable by neither what came before nor what comes after, hence unnameable — from merely recalling one from rehearsal. Quoting Keith's tribute to Dylan's pre-electric float against the 'relentless discipline of a rhythm section,' he lays out the standard skeleton of kick on beats one and three, snare slap on two and four. The tiniest rushing or relaxing of the four beats in mutual relation decides whether a groove is erotic and invigorating or limpid.

chapters.file: ch91 - Alright Now.md
chapters.relation: Auxier inventories Keith's original grooves: the 'Start Me Up' riff, the one-one-one-one kick-in of 'Jumpin' Jack Flash,' the agonizingly slow 'Honky Tonk Women,' the slowest rock groove he knows in 'Wild Horses,' with 'Beast of Burden' credited to Charlie and 'Shattered' likely to Bill. He argues no single person has contributed more previously undiscovered grooves to rock, with Chuck Berry the only rival, whose songs collapse unless played in exactly the right groove. Musicians themselves name these grooves by their Stones songs.

chapters.file: ch92 - Riffing.md
chapters.relation: Auxier analyzes the riff's first leg, tone: the endless knob-and-amplifier experimentation needed to make 'Nineteenth Nervous Breakdown' feel like what it is, with Keith as the creator of unique, deliberately unrepeatable tones like the 'Satisfaction' fuzz. He recounts Keith's revelation that 'Jumpin' Jack Flash' used no electric guitars at all — acoustics overloaded into a Phillips cassette recorder's built-in mic — proving clean sound isn't always the best sound. Rock guitarists, he says, must go to school on the tones Keith made.

chapters.file: ch93 - You Make a Dead Man . ..md
chapters.relation: Auxier completes the riff with the 'sig lick,' the signature phrase — a violin arpeggio in 'Ruby Tuesday,' a melodic figure in 'Nineteenth Nervous Breakdown,' the six ascending notes before 'brown sugar' — that identifies a song within a couple of seconds. The sig lick is the culmination of pulling the lightning down, making the listener lose herself in anticipation and memory, dying a little death in the moment. He credits Keith and his rhythm section with perhaps six dozen one-of-a-kind winning riffs, presciently recognized as such.

chapters.file: ch94 - The Singer, Not the Song.md
chapters.relation: Auxier separates Keith's guitar greatness from songwriting: riffs and grooves often occasioned the songs Jagger voiced, and the same song can carry different grooves, as the Folksmen's bluegrass 'Start Me Up' proves painfully. Keith's real feat was exploring the terra incognita of sounds the electric guitar first made hearable by human ears, demanding curiosity, tenacity and focus. To deny his greatness, Auxier says, is like saying Christopher Columbus wasn't a great sea captain.

chapters.file: ch95 - A Steady Synthesis of the Data.md
chapters.relation: Auxier confesses he long judged Charlie Watts a mediocre drummer with hitches, jerks and an annoying snare-only habit on beats two and four, measuring him against conscious, conventional expectations of technique. Whitehead's dictum that consciousness is rare and unimportant reframes Charlie as the second phase of Stones concrescence, pulling the whole together beneath the radar of theory. The life lesson: when something is very good and your pet theory says it shouldn't be, dump the theory.

chapters.file: ch96 - The River of Tight.md
chapters.relation: Auxier argues there is a kind of looseness on the far side of tight, distinguishing the Grateful Dead's chosen wildness beyond the 'River of Tight' from the Stones' well-chosen spots just past it. Tight playing is cerebral — music for Rush, Styx, Kansas and Yes — impressive to the ears and head but not to the ass and feet. The moral reaches past music: life cannot go to plan once you step on stage, so learn tightness, then forget it and live in the moment.

chapters.file: ch97 - Charlie Chuckles.md
chapters.relation: Auxier reveals Charlie Watts's secret: he lags behind Keith's front-edge attack to the last possible micromoment, then lands a comic, jocular snort just beyond it, releasing Keith's manic intensity as levity — that is 'when the whip comes down.' 'Beast of Burden' exemplifies the design, its oodles of empty sonic space created by Charlie hopping to the front of the beat and falling way back every measure, as the near-random double snare slap exposes how far he has trailed. Keith's autobiography confirms the two test each other's rhythmic limits for fun.

chapters.file: ch98 - Paying the Bill An Ode to Satisfaction.md
chapters.relation: Auxier reads Bill Wyman as the rhythm section's distributor of joy who was personally 'not destined for satisfaction,' the older man who never quite bought in. Bill's genius was refusing to lock with Charlie's kick drum, instead lagging behind even Charlie and bringing each bar back to Keith's root — a thick, deep four-string memory that realizes Whitehead's 'satisfaction,' the phase where what is made culminates and contributes to what comes next. 'Miss You' is his masterpiece of playing in the interstices, while 'Paint It Black' is the rare exception where the bass drives the backbeat.

chapters.file: ch99 - What a Mess!.md
chapters.relation: Auxier reads 'Shattered' as a menacing tangle of bottom-end dissonance made for the gonads and solar plexus rather than the ear, with Bill's bass shutting the door behind the band — though never again after 1992. He then answers the chapter's opening promise about what rock destroys: ourselves, our youth, sacrificed on its altar. Naming Freud's thanatos, the death wish beneath the organized energies, he defines rocking as wanting to stop your own heart every four beats and find resurrection on the far side of the bar.

chapters.file: ch100 - Chapter 11 - The Stones in Pepperland.md
chapters.relation: Bill Martin opens Chapter 11 by joking that Hegel's dialectical Reason and Marx's class conflict both missed the universe's most revealing tension: Beatles versus Stones. He dismantles the 'bad boys' and working-class image as confused — the Beatles were no posh outfit, and The Who could have taken both bands in a street brawl. He concedes, though, that musically the Beatles 'kicked all of their butts' with Sgt. Pepper.

chapters.file: ch101 - Please Pass the Pepper.md
chapters.relation: Martin coins 'Pepperism' for the mid-sixties moment when rock, spurred by Miles Davis, Coltrane and Coleman in jazz, Cage and Stockhausen in classical music, and non-Western musics, broke its founding blues framework, with Sgt. Pepper making experimentation the main trend centered on 1968. Against it he sets the 'blues orthodoxy' reaction — 'that ain't rock'n'roll' — which turns the Beatles and Stones into genuine rivals over what rock should be. Yet in 1967 the bands briefly agreed on experimentation, and the result was Their Satanic Majesties Request.

chapters.file: ch102 - It’s Only Their Satanic Majesties Request, But . ..md
chapters.relation: Martin weighs Keith's dismissal of Majesties as a 'put-on' and 'flimflam' against the album's value, arguing it reveals the Stones' genuine dark side — invoking Satan where the Beatles never would — and seals the case that the Stones were less innovative perfectionists, since an attempted Sgt. Pepper was bound to fail. Invoking Badiou's claim that every artist has at most one great idea, he grants the Stones' idea is blues-plus-rock, which Majesties is not. Still he prefers listening to it: its Ginsberg-like 'first thought, best thought' mess gives it an edginess the polished Pepper lacks, making 'really cool' a candidate aesthetic category.

chapters.file: ch103 - In the Court of the Satanic Majesty.md
chapters.relation: Martin situates the Stones amid Pepperist experimentation — Jagger's film work with Roeg and Anger, and King Crimson's mind-blowing set opening the 1969 Hyde Park memorial for Brian Jones. The Stones' own ragged Hyde Park performance pointed to their turn away from Pepperism and back to the blues. He nonetheless argues Majesties should be seen as the Stones' only true concept album — indeed a 'concepts album' that prog fans should heed.

chapters.file: ch104 - Beelzebub’s Bugged-Out Bequest.md
chapters.relation: Martin identifies two threads in Majesties, hippie-utopianism and science fiction, reading the sorcerer Robes cover as what he calls 'sci-fi medievalism' and tracing four songs. 'Citadel' erupts from dissonance into a Bastille-like prison; 'In Another Land' is a utopian dream-within-a-dream whose 'Is this some kind of joke?' anticipates the paranoid machine-consciousness of The Matrix and Philip K. Dick's VALIS; Bill Wyman's '2000 Man' has an affair with a computer; and '2000 Light Years from Home' goes beyond Pepperism itself. The band stood, like rock between Woodstock and Altamont, poised between utopia and dystopia.

chapters.file: ch105 - You’re So Very Lonely.md
chapters.relation: Martin reads the album's science-fiction songs as studies in loneliness, isolation and alienation, the paired '2000' titles marking time and distance rather than literal measures. The closer 'On With the Show' turns Pepper's emcee routine into a cynical scam — 'we've got all the answers' — that deflates the utopian optimism of 'Sing This All Together' and anticipates the anti-utopian note of Lennon's 'Revolution' and Townshend's 'Won't Get Fooled Again.' He locates the album as ground tilled for Zappa's parody We're Only in It for the Money.

chapters.file: ch106 - 2000 Light Years from the Blues.md
chapters.relation: Martin shows the Stones disowned Majesties themselves — Mick's interpretive dance on the 1989 '2000 Light Years from Home' strips out the alienation and re-blueses the rhythm — concluding the Stones never belonged in Pepperland. The 3-D cover strands them without the carnival of artists and intellectuals that contextualizes Pepper's collage; their real idols were Muddy Waters and Screamin' Jay Hawkins, who would have looked as absurd there as 'Hey You, Get Off of My Nebula.' Their experimentalism was secondhand, taken at one remove from Sgt. Pepper, though it paid off for later bands like the Brian Jonestown Massacre.

chapters.file: ch107 - Chapter 12 - Beatles versus Stones The Last Word.md
chapters.relation: Crispin Sartwell opens Chapter 12 by deflating the Beatles-versus-Stones debate and the modernist genius-cult that made it possible: Beethoven, Van Gogh, Nietzsche, Picasso and Joyce imagined as transcendent, 'God-touched' geniuses whose actual music is absurdly inadequate to the adulation. Great-figure narratives, he argues, simplify history into nodes and satisfy the impulse to worship, while promotion of any actual person to that status is nearly arbitrary. No one, he insists, is as far above everyone else as the Beatles are imagined to be.

chapters.file: ch108 - Avant the Avant-Garde.md
chapters.relation: Sartwell distinguishes avant-garde art, which authenticates itself through radical negations of the past (impressionism through conceptualism), from traditional arts like country and blues, which authenticate through continuity, apprenticeship and settled forms such as the twelve-bar structure. Innovators from Robert Johnson to Hendrix change these traditions while preserving an underlying continuity, though Hendrix's shredded, burned blues licks poise him between tradition and avant-garde. Early rock'n'roll — Chuck Berry, Elvis — emerges as both eclectic and traditional, a syncretic blend of black and white southern styles.

chapters.file: ch109 - Salt of the Earth.md
chapters.relation: Sartwell recalls Keith and Mick bonding as obsessive blues-record archivists and notes both early bands were essentially cover bands performing American black music for European audiences, the Beatles' 'Twist and Shout' the best such appropriation. He refuses to condemn white appropriations of black styles — no race owns art, and figures from Bix Beiderbecke to Elvis often revived, paid, and popularized the artists they venerated. African-American forms, he argues, have been the source of the world's popular music for a century, down to the participatory behavior of rock audiences.

chapters.file: ch110 - The Riff Not Taken.md
chapters.relation: Sartwell contrasts the bands' moral personae: the wholesome Beatles of A Hard Day's Night and 'All You Need Is Love' versus the Stones flirting with Satan in Majesties and 'Sympathy for the Devil' and ending at Altamont, a good-boy/bad-boy split he likens to the Madonna-whore complex. The real divergence is musical: the Beatles developed a new vocabulary and became avant-garde artists, while the Stones, however sharper and more original, kept referring back to the rock, soul and blues vocabularies they started with, developing like a traditional art.

chapters.file: ch111 - You’re 2000 Light Years from Home.md
chapters.relation: Sartwell dates the Beatles' avant-garde turn from Rubber Soul through Sgt. Pepper: a shift from blues tonality to British music-hall colors, orchestral and sitar instrumentation, and surreal lyrics like 'Glass Onion,' making 'Yesterday' a category mistake of a rock song. He judges much of the Revolver-to-Let It Be output overblown yet trivial — 'Mr. Kite' is no Guernica — and blames messianic audience worship ('bigger than Jesus') for the band's self-indulgence. The turn, he charges, produced the soulless anti-rock of Elton John and Billy Joel and the empty art-rock of Yes and ELP.

chapters.file: ch112 - Let the Blues Be.md
chapters.relation: Sartwell declares the Stones 'a cosmic essence, a Platonic Form, of rock music': where the Beatles passed through mannerist, baroque and rococo decadence to an aesthetic dead end, Keith stripped the rock lick to its essence from 'Satisfaction' through 'Gunface.' Invoking Plato's view that Forms are remembered and discovered — essences that are both our origin and our destiny — he argues the Stones reverted continually to the origins of their music in blues, country and soul while exposing the center of the center. Beggar's Banquet through Exile on Main Street, he proposes, just is rock music, achieving one's own essence as a legitimate aesthetic project.

chapters.file: ch113 - IV - Politics Sexual and the Other Kind.md
ch114 - Chapter 13 - You Can’t Always Get What You Want.md
chapters.relation: Luke Dick opens Chapter 13 with Sartre's 1947 line about marriage taboos versus contraceptives in college back yards and sets Western monogamy — inherited through church and institutions, with divorce thanks to Henry VIII — against the Stones' womanizing image, 'Some Girls' included. A timeline frames the test: Sartre and Beauvoir's 1927 pact of open love, Jagger fashioning himself Don Juan incarnate ('Sexually, yes. Financially, no. Philosophically, trying'), Charlie Watts' steadfast 1964 marriage, and Keith stealing Anita from Brian Jones. The chapter asks whether humans are cut out for monogamy at all.

chapters.file: ch115 - Saw Her Today at the Reception.md
chapters.relation: Dick reads 'You Can't Always Get What You Want' as an anatomy of wanting to keep something and let it go at once, locating the revelation not in Mr. Jimmy or the demonstration but in the reception scene, where Mick confronts that love will never fulfill his expectations. He generalizes to ordinary life: domestic routine can blissfully stabilize a meaningful life or leave the heart 'looking bored behind the drum set,' and rock stardom's surfeit of mates only multiplies the strain. This raises the chapter's governing question — what is a tradition, and should it dictate anything?

chapters.file: ch116 - A Footloose Man.md
chapters.relation: Dick expounds Sartre's 'Existentialism Is a Humanism' through the essentialist picture — a God-given blueprint, like Keith's Bentley designed before manufacture — against Sartre's claim that we exist first and invent essences afterward, marriage and family included. Monogamy thus emerges as a human choice mandated by Western authority and imposed on conquered peoples, not an absolute ethic handed down from heaven, a freedom humans exercise even in dropping Deuteronomy's stoning rule. Keith, Mick and Simone discarded the inherited tradition of monogamy, while Charlie Watts chose to stick with it.

chapters.file: ch117 - Practiced at the Art of Deception.md
chapters.relation: Dick diagnoses Jagger's contradiction: he wants to be both knight and sorcerer, accepted by the aristocratic tradition while living out 'Some Girls,' but you cannot be establishment and counterculture at once. The pendulum swings from sleeping with Keith's girlfriend Anita — passion fulfilled, tradition left a vacuous hole — back home to Marianne while he craves the next mistress. This incongruous moral bearings problem guarantees Mick's unfulfillment, the very tension 'You Can't Always Get What You Want' sings of.

chapters.file: ch118 - Glass of Wine in Her Hand.md
chapters.relation: Dick portraits Keith as Bacchus incarnate, guided by camaraderie and a will for collective hedonistic comfort rather than any defined moral impulse, with romantic and platonic lines blurred — everyone nearby drinks the vapors from his cauldron. The chaos works inside the circle but turns deadly on contact with a world that needs yellow lines: Marlon running amok on the '76 tour, partners straying while Keith passes out. His verdict: Keith would be dead if he hadn't been a Rolling Stone.

chapters.file: ch119 - If You Try Sometimes . ..md
chapters.relation: Dick closes with Charlie Watts near seventy, married to Shirley Ann Shepherd since 1964, whose only indulgence at Hugh Hefner's Playboy mansion in 1972 was the billiard room. He weighs explanations — little impulse for sexual diversity, indifference to passion's initial stages, or resilience compelled by promises and tradition — while admitting marriages are tense, burning things where fatigue is common. Watts endures as he drums: he doesn't drop the beat when his arms get tired.

holes.name: Alfred North Whitehead
holes.what: Process philosopher who saw reality as rhythmic bursts of energy and events rather than enduring substances.
holes.why: Chapter 85 introduces Whitehead's process philosophy as the framework for explaining the 'It' that lets the Stones channel energy, and he anchors all of Chapter 10.

holes.name: Process Philosophy (concrescence)
holes.what: Whitehead's view that reality consists of rhythmic events or 'actual occasions' (datum, synthesis, satisfaction) rather than static things.
holes.why: Chapter 86 maps the Stones' rhythm section onto Whitehead's phases of concrescence to explain why the band rocks, the central argument of the whole unit.

holes.name: Self-Creative Act
holes.what: Whitehead's notion of an act of experience that creates itself, not wholly explained by what came before or after it.
holes.why: Chapter 90 uses the self-creative act to explain how novel grooves are discovered and why they resist being named.

holes.name: Thanatos (the Death Drive)
holes.what: Freud's concept of a death instinct or death wish operating beneath the life drives.
holes.why: Chapter 99 invokes thanatos to explain the 'little death' and the sacrifice of youth at the rhythmic heart of rock.

holes.name: Cultural Appropriation
holes.what: The adoption of another culture's artistic forms by outsiders, contested over credit, exploitation and power.
holes.why: Chapter 109's central ethical question is whether white musicians like the Beatles and Stones wrongfully appropriated Black American music.
